[b]The Commonwealth & Verdant[/b]

The first official call for negotiations between the Commonwealth of High Albany and the Tri-State of Verdant came in the form of a formal address from the Office of the Director. For years, discussions of Pan-Albicism had circulated among scholars, political commentators, and economic strategists, but now, with shifting geopolitical interests and growing public sentiment, the moment had arrived to take concrete steps. The government in Kingsmount issued a diplomatic overture, inviting Verdants leadership to consider formal negotiations for reentry into the Commonwealth. Though previously a part of the greater Albic polity before the Directory and the Unification War, Verdant had remained independent for generations, maintaining a strong agrarian economy and a vital oil industry. However, economic integration with the broader Commonwealth had never truly ceased. Trade agreements, cultural exchanges, and political alignments had kept the bonds between Verdant and the Commonwealth intact, if unofficial.

The initial response from Verdant was cautious but receptive. The Tri-State had long debated the benefits and drawbacks of closer alignment with High Albany. Their government, composed of representatives from West Verdant, Old Verdant, and East Verdant, had always maintained a pragmatic stance regarding external relations. While Verdant valued its sovereignty, economic pressures and shifting regional alliances had made the prospect of reunification increasingly attractive. Preliminary talks began with private discussions between Verdants Chief Minister and High Albanys Minister of Foreign Affairs, held in a neutral setting to gauge interest and explore potential avenues for cooperation. The meetings were deliberately low-profile, ensuring that both governments could feel out each other's positions before making any public commitments.

As word of the discussions leaked, public interest surged across both nations. In High Albany, news outlets framed the negotiations as a historic opportunity to restore Albic unity, emphasizing the economic and cultural advantages of reintegration. The idea of a reunified Albic Peninsula, with Verdant leading the way for other Albic nations, gained traction. Public polling conducted by the Kingsmount Institute of Policy Studies indicated that nearly 70% of Commonwealth citizens supported Verdants return, with only minor opposition from isolationist factions. Meanwhile, in Verdant, public sentiment was mixed. Older generations, still wary of past conflicts, were hesitant, while younger voters, eager for greater economic opportunities and modern infrastructure, overwhelmingly supported the prospect. Political factions in Verdant began to form around the issue, with the National Unity Party endorsing reintegration and the Sovereignty Front voicing concerns over potential loss of independence.

To formalize discussions, the Commonwealth invited Verdants delegation to Kingsmount for a summit. The event was carefully orchestrated, emphasizing shared history and mutual benefit. Symbolic gestures were prominentnegotiations were hosted in the Old Assembly Hall, the same chamber where representatives from Verdant had once sat before their secession. The Director personally welcomed the delegation, reinforcing the message that Verdant had always been considered an integral part of the greater Albic community. The opening speeches were diplomatic but direct, outlining the benefits of reintegration: economic security, military protection, and access to the vast financial and technological resources of the Commonwealth.

Behind closed doors, negotiations focused on key issues. Verdants representatives sought guarantees of regional autonomy, ensuring that West Verdant, Old Verdant, and East Verdant would retain a degree of self-governance under the Commonwealths federal structure. Economic arrangements were also central, with Verdant demanding favorable terms on trade, taxation, and subsidies to modernize infrastructure. High Albany, in turn, required commitments to democratic governance, adherence to constitutional law, and participation in federal decision-making. These were complex matters, requiring extensive deliberation.

Meanwhile, both governments worked to shape public perception. In the Commonwealth, the government launched a campaign emphasizing unity, stability, and prosperity. Media outlets were encouraged to highlight Verdants historical ties to High Albany, broadcasting documentaries on shared cultural heritage and publishing opinion pieces from economists and political scientists advocating for reintegration. Billboards in major cities carried slogans such as "One People, One Future" and "Verdants Place is in the Commonwealth."

In Verdant, the approach was more measured. Given the divided public opinion, the government initiated town hall meetings across all three states, allowing citizens to voice concerns and ask questions. Government-affiliated think tanks published reports outlining the benefits of joining, focusing on economic growth, infrastructure investment, and increased international influence. Opponents of reintegration were not ignored; debates were held, and opposition voices were given space in newspapers and broadcasts to ensure the process remained transparent and democratic.

The first major legislative step came when the Verdant Assembly voted to formally enter negotiations with the Commonwealth. The vote was contentious, passing with a 58-42 split, reflecting ongoing divisions. However, once approved, the process accelerated. Both sides committed to a structured timeline, setting key milestones for agreements on governance, economics, and military integration.

With negotiations moving forward, the Commonwealths Parliament prepared to debate the conditions of Verdants admission. Some representatives argued for an expedited process, fearing that delays could jeopardize momentum. Others urged caution, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive and mutually beneficial agreement. Committees were formed to review economic implications, legal adjustments, and foreign policy considerations. Meanwhile, diplomatic envoys were dispatched to other Albic nations, gauging their reactions and preparing the groundwork for future expansions.

With the formal negotiation process in motion, the focus shifted from broad agreements to the finer details of reintegration. Both the Commonwealth and the Tri-State of Verdant established working groups composed of legal experts, economists, military advisors, and political representatives to draft the framework for Verdants reentry. These committees worked under intense scrutiny, knowing that every clause would be dissected by both the Verdant Assembly and the Commonwealth Parliament.

The first major challenge came in defining Verdants administrative status within the Commonwealths federal system. While Verdants leadership accepted the broader structure of nation, state, province, county, and district, they sought assurances that West Verdant, Old Verdant, and East Verdant would retain significant autonomy over local governance. The Commonwealth negotiators countered with a model that aligned Verdants new states with existing member states, ensuring parity in representation while maintaining provincial and county-level control over internal affairs. After weeks of deliberation, a compromise was reached: Verdant would join as three separate states, each with its own governor, state legislature, and administrative framework, but all bound by federal laws and policies.

Simultaneously, economic discussions intensified. Verdants representatives pushed for transitionary economic protections, fearing that sudden integration into the Commonwealths larger and more competitive market could disrupt local industries. The Commonwealth, while eager to bring Verdant fully into its economic system, recognized the need for gradual alignment. A phased approach was agreed uponVerdants agricultural and oil sectors would receive temporary subsidies, and local businesses would be granted a five-year adjustment period before being fully subjected to federal tax structures. Additionally, the Commonwealth pledged major infrastructure investments, promising new rail connections, modernized highways, and expanded energy grids to integrate Verdant seamlessly into the greater economic network.

One of the most delicate issues was military integration. Verdant, despite its small size, maintained an independent defense force, with its own command structure and territorial security policies. The Commonwealth required full military integration, but Verdants leadership sought guarantees that their forces would not be immediately dissolved. After protracted negotiations, an agreement was reached wherein Verdants existing forces would be merged into the Commonwealth Armed Forces over a seven-year period, with officers given pathways into Commonwealth command structures and Verdants strategic assets incorporated into the broader defense network.

Public discourse surrounding the negotiations grew increasingly intense. In the Commonwealth, the government maintained its messaging on unity and economic prosperity, but opposition voices began to emerge, particularly from isolationist factions and those skeptical of the economic costs of integration. Some argued that Verdants agricultural protections and subsidies placed an unfair burden on Commonwealth taxpayers. In response, government officials released detailed economic projections demonstrating the long-term benefits of reintegration, including increased trade, expanded resource access, and enhanced geopolitical stability.

In Verdant, the political landscape remained deeply divided. The Sovereignty Front intensified its efforts, warning that joining the Commonwealth would result in the erosion of local traditions and political independence. They held rallies across Verdant, emphasizing national pride and cautioning against outside influence. In contrast, the National Unity Party, now leading the integration effort, promoted a vision of economic modernization and greater global influence. To sway public opinion, the Verdant government launched an information campaign, detailing the benefits of Commonwealth membership, including expanded social services, infrastructure projects, and economic security.

With negotiations nearing completion, both nations prepared for legislative votes. In Verdant, the Assembly scheduled a national referendum, allowing citizens to directly decide their future. The campaign period was marked by intense debates, public forums, and media campaigns from both sides. Polling suggested a narrow but growing majority in favor of reintegration, with younger voters and business leaders strongly supportive, while rural communities remained skeptical.

In the Commonwealth, the Parliament debated the conditions of Verdants admission. Some lawmakers pushed for a more stringent integration timeline, while others sought additional economic safeguards to ensure Verdants transition did not disrupt Commonwealth industries. After lengthy deliberations, the Parliament passed the Verdant Reentry Act, formally outlining the terms of admission and setting a date for final ratification, contingent on Verdants referendum outcome.

On the day of the referendum, voter turnout in Verdant reached historic levels. Ballot stations were overwhelmed with citizens eager to cast their votes, and international observers monitored the process to ensure fairness. As results were tallied, tensions ran high. Finally, after a full night of counting, the official result was announced58% in favor, 42% against. The decision was clear: Verdant would rejoin the Commonwealth.

The announcement sparked celebrations in major cities, with supporters gathering in town squares and waving both Verdant and Commonwealth flags. In Kingsmount, the Director issued a formal statement, welcoming Verdant back into the fold and affirming the Commonwealths commitment to a smooth and prosperous reintegration. Meanwhile, opposition voices in Verdant accepted the result but vowed to ensure that the new relationship with the Commonwealth remained fair and balanced.

With the referendums results clear, the final phase of Verdants reintegration into the Commonwealth began in earnest. Both governments moved swiftly to formalize the agreements, ensuring a smooth transition that would satisfy both legislative bodies and the wider public. The Commonwealth Parliament, having already passed the Verdant Reentry Act, now focused on enacting supplementary provisions that would accommodate Verdants phased economic and military integration. Meanwhile, the Verdant Assembly prepared to dissolve portions of its independent legal and administrative frameworks to align with Commonwealth governance structures.

The official signing ceremony was scheduled to take place in Kingsmount, the capital of the Commonwealth, at the Grand Parliament Hall. Representatives from both governments, key negotiators, and invited dignitaries from across the Albic Peninsula were in attendance. The occasion carried immense historical weightVerdants departure from the Commonwealth had been a defining event of the Directory and Unification War, and now, generations later, it was the first breakaway state to return voluntarily. The treaties were signed with great ceremony, solidifying Verdants three new statesWest Verdant, Old Verdant, and East Verdantwithin the federal structure of the Commonwealth.

Despite the celebrations, the work of reintegration had only just begun. One of the most immediate priorities was the realignment of Verdants administrative systems. Officials from both sides coordinated efforts to transition Verdants governmental departments into the Commonwealth framework. State legislatures were formally established, new governors were appointed, and representatives from the three Verdant states prepared for their first participation in Commonwealth parliamentary elections.

Economically, the agreed-upon subsidies and adjustment period went into effect. The Commonwealths central bank worked closely with Verdants financial institutions to facilitate currency standardization and ensure stability in markets and trade agreements. Infrastructure projects were fast-trackedrailways and highways linking Verdant to the Commonwealth heartland saw immediate upgrades, and investments were funneled into modernizing Verdants industrial and agricultural sectors.

Military integration proceeded according to the negotiated seven-year timeline. Verdants existing forces were gradually brought under the command of the Commonwealth Armed Forces, with training programs established to align military protocols. Officers from Verdant were given the opportunity to retain their ranks while adapting to the Commonwealths structure, and Verdants strategic defense assets were incorporated into the national security framework.

As reintegration progressed, the Commonwealth government launched initiatives to foster national unity and strengthen cultural ties. Public events celebrated Verdants return, and educational campaigns highlighted the shared history and values of the Albic peoples. The media played a significant role in reinforcing the message of unity, with newspapers, radio, and television broadcasting stories about Verdants historical role in the Albic Peninsula and its future within the Commonwealth.

In Verdant, opposition voices, though accepting the referendum results, continued to express concerns about the pace of integration and the preservation of local identity. The Sovereignty Front, while diminished in influence, advocated for ongoing vigilance to ensure that Verdants interests were not overshadowed by the larger Commonwealth. The government of Verdant, now operating within the Commonwealth system, assured citizens that state rights and local governance would be protected, and that the transition would not erase Verdants distinct character.

Within almost a year, Verdants first representatives were seated in the Commonwealth Parliament, marking the full political reintegration of the region. While challenges remained, the process had been largely peaceful and orderly, serving as a model for other Albic states considering rejoining the Commonwealth. Discussions within the Albic Peninsula intensified, with neighboring independent states now facing increasing pressure to follow Verdants path, at least politically if not financially due how well the three Verdants are doing.

Meantime, Director William Blythe got into a bit of a controversy after allegations he had more than thoroughly enjoyed the company of one of the Verdantic female ambassadors who had made up the diplomatic entourage of the negations, it is however doubtful if rumours are true or not, it seems unlikely it'll affect his political career. On another topic, Verdant's Spring, a soda company that makes a delicious lemon flavoured transparent soda has begun sweeping into the market after it was permitted to, with many enjoying on the beverage to honour the reconciliation and unification between the Commonwealth and the Tri-state, although many note it might be too gaseous for some, although others take it up as a challenge, the Verdant Challenge, of seeing how many one can take without burping.

Spring stocks are rising because of this, further more it seems overall Commonwealth company's stocks are rising as well through the unification and the merging of the economic system, as the Verdantic companies engrain themselves into the Commonwealth competitive economy. In the meantime there have been reports of some movie directors and other journalists trying to make a timeline of events and meetings as well as dialogue and niche about the entire unification process, with rumours saying perhaps a movie, all likely comedic with a bit of thrill, might be independently made by some more renowned movie directors, some people hoping Director Blythe might make a cameo on it, or other such officials.

[b]OF ANGELS AND MORTALS[/b]
[i]Prologue: The First Awakening[/i]

STARBOUND: 2500]
A large object is hurtling through the Great Beyond. It is no bigger than the moon of the First Planet.

The rogue moon enters the orbit of one of the planets in the area. The planet it has come into contact with is nothing more than an endless ocean; it would be the impact of this object that would give it its first landforms and kickstart the birth of all life on this particular planet in the Great Beyond.

The moon begins to inch closer and closer to the surface of this planet. Its orbit is decaying; it doesn't have enough strength to fight the pull of the planet's gravity. 

It finally crashes into the planet. On impact, the moon digs a giant gash into the ocean, tearing itself to pieces as it does so. Eventually, what little is left of the moon comes to rest.

From the remains of the shattered moon, a gargantuan creature rises. Its size is unfathomable; it towers high above the planet and the top of its head reaches the edge of the atmosphere. Its shape is identifiably human, but yet its not - its arms are as long as its body and it stands on its toes, like an animal. A single, giant eye rests in the centre of its head.

The creature looks around, taking in all the details of its new home. 

For the kind of race it is supposed to create, the conditions of this planet are downright unsuitable. 

The creature kneels down, and begins to scoop up humongous chunks of stone, dirt and mud. Its hands breathe life into the soil; every chunk it picks up begins to sprout plant life from all corners.

The creature forms a massive, flat island from the ocean. It rests one of its hands on the island, and from the tips of its fingers, creatures a thousand times smaller than it emerge. These creatures stand upright on two legs, and are covered from head to toe in hairless skin. They're almost animalistic in the way they act in their first moments of life, yet the way they move is with purpose and intention.

They are intelligent, just like the creature they arose from.

All of a sudden, another moon comes crashing down onto the planet. The creature is startled by this. It looks around, trying to find the place where this moon has come to rest. Eventually, it manages to find the location of this moon.

It is scared, but still curious. It cautiously approaches the shattered moon, looking for a sign of life in the celestial rubble.

Before the creature can react, a beast jumps out of the moon and tackles it into the ocean with a spear clamped around the creature's neck. The assailant looks like a canine, and like the creature, it stands on two legs and has arms that are as long as its body. It has three pairs of eyes, stacked one after the other on its head.

The creature attempts to fight back against the beast. It tries to take the beast's spear off its neck, but it is forced down again. It is simply too weak to fight back.

The beast lifts the spear and stabs it directly into the collar of the creature. The creature howls in agony, and in desperation forces itself back up onto its legs. It tears the spear out of its body, and begins to battle the beast with it. The beast suddenly grabs the spear, and yanks it out of the creature's hand. With the spear's blunt end, the beast whacks the creature hard, and sends it flying across the planet, back to the island it had formed. The creature lands on its back on the island, crushing all of its children in the process.

It tries to get up, but before it can it is impaled by the beast's spear. It falls back down onto the surface, writhing in agony and pain from the beast's attacks.

The beast takes a giant leap, and lunges at the creature. It grabs its spear, and forces it deeper into the creature. It is now pinned to the ground, unable to move. The beast begins to maul the creature, tearing it to shreds in a fit of fury and absolute bloodthirsty rage. Chunks of the creature go flying everywhere, landing in different parts of the world.

The beast arches its back, and lets out a deafening roar of victory.

...

[i]Uriel. The angel of wisdom. Armed with nothing but his wits. The Seed of Man.

Zeruel. The angel of strength. Armed with the Spear of Fire. The Seed of the Beast.

Sahaquiel. The angel of the sky. Armed with the Wings of Light. The Seed of the Sky.

Sachiel. The angel of water. Armed with the Lance of Righteousness. The Seed of the Marine.

The four primal beings of the First Order. The means of which they disseminated life into the Great Beyond. All of them create sapient beings. They can cooperate, as they did once on the First Planet, but more often than not they enter into active battle against one another if they have arrived on the same planet.

The human genome died with Uriel on Eiridia.

By the will of Zeruel, what was intended to be the second human planet in the Great Beyond became the second planet of the Anima.

From Him arose the Kanes, Eiridia's dominant race.[/i]
[/spoiler]
